title: the Sri Sukta
hook: the hymn wants the goddess of fortune in the house, and the first one it speaks to is the fire

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta opened with a portrait: golden, garlanded in gold and silver, shining like the moon.

There's an old way to meet someone important: don't knock on their door yourself. Ask someone who already knows them, a cousin, a teacher, a friend of a friend, to make the introduction and bring you by. The Sri Sukta does exactly that. The singer wants Sri, the goddess of fortune, in the house. But the first words of request aren't spoken to her at all. They're spoken to the fire. Today, the end of that opening verse. Bring her to me, fire.
screen: `ASK SOMEONE WHO KNOWS THEM.` → `THE FIRST REQUEST ISN'T TO HER.` → `BRING HER TO ME, FIRE.`

segments.voice: The verse ends, in paraphrase: O Jatavedas, bring Lakshmi to me. Jatavedas is a name of Agni, the fire. Start with what the fire does in the Vedas. In the opening hymn of the Rig Veda, Agni is praised as the priest of the sacrifice, the one who will bring the gods here. Offerings go into the fire, and the fire brings the gods. Fire is the go-between. So when the Sri Sukta asks the fire to bring Lakshmi, it's asking fire to do its old work. Second, the little word for bring: avaha, bring here, carry this way. It isn't go and get. It's closer to a host saying to a friend: please bring her by. The singer stays home, keeps the fire going, and trusts the fire to make the introduction. Third, what's quietly assumed. You can't ask a fire for anything if none is burning. A household fire needs fuel, care and someone to watch it, and the request depends on that steady small work. Some readers hear a plain lesson in it: fortune is asked for through something you already keep alive at home. Fourth, the lamp. In some Hindu homes, small lamps are lit when Lakshmi is welcomed, especially at Diwali, the festival this path met in its first year, along windowsills and doorsteps. The go-between is now small enough to sit in a clay cup. Great altar or one wick in oil, the shape of the request is the same: a light is kept burning, and the goddess is asked to come by it.
screen: `JATAVEDAS: A NAME OF AGNI, THE FIRE.` · `FIRE IS THE GO-BETWEEN.` · `AVAHA: PLEASE BRING HER BY.` · `A FIRE THAT SOMEONE KEEPS.` · then, large: `BRING LAKSHMI TO ME.`

segments.voice: Picture a small household fire, low and steady: with each in-breath, lay one small stick on it; with each out-breath, watch it settle and glow, not too much, not too little. If you pray, you can ask the fire, as the hymn does, to bring good fortune to your house, or speak to God in your own words; if you don't, let the flame stand for whatever you hope will come.
The Sri Sukta. In its opening verse, the singer asks Jatavedas, the fire, to bring Lakshmi: the fire as the go-between.
Your line: the Sri Sukta. A light kept burning, and a guest asked to come by it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Lakshmi worship and Vedic rites, the Sri Sukta is chanted before a lamp or sacred fire, and some households light small lamps at Diwali to welcome the goddess.

chat.says: If the Sri Sukta wants Lakshmi, why does it talk to the fire first?
options: In the Vedas, fire is the go-between who brings the gods, so it's asked to bring her.
Because Lakshmi is afraid of fire, and the singer asks it to step aside for her.
Because fire guards Lakshmi's door, so the singer must ask its permission first.
chat.meaning: Jatavedas is a name of Agni. In the Rig Veda, Agni brings the gods to the sacrifice, so the singer asks fire to bring Lakshmi.

notes: Sri Sukta 1 paraphrased (jātavedo ma āvaha). Day 1092 (another writer) also explains Jatavedas briefly as the fire who carries offerings; an editor may trim one of the two.
